stem: What does it mean to separate deploying from releasing?
options: Deploying on weekends and releasing on weekdays
Getting new code running in production where few or no users see it, then exposing it gradually - by traffic share, audience or feature flag - so it can be withdrawn quickly
Keeping the code in a release branch until it is approved
Deploying only infrastructure, never application code
explanation: When deploying and releasing are the same moment, every deployment is a bet on all users. Slots, canaries, rings and flags let new code run and be observed first, and make withdrawing it fast.

scenario: Rolling back last Tuesday's release meant rebuilding the previous commit and redeploying it, which took 40 minutes.
stem: Which approach makes rollback take seconds for the API on App Service?
options: Keep a zip of the last build on a laptop
Deploy to a staging slot and swap; the previous version stays in the staging slot, so swapping back is the rollback
Deploy directly to production faster
Scale out before each release
explanation: After a swap, the previous version is still running, warm, in the other slot. Swapping back restores it in seconds, with no rebuild or cold start.

stem: What distinguishes a canary release from a blue-green switch?
options: A canary uses a different region
A canary sends a small share of real traffic to the new version first and increases it only if metrics hold; blue-green switches all traffic at once
A canary needs no monitoring
Blue-green cannot be rolled back
explanation: Canaries limit how many users are exposed while the new version proves itself on real traffic. Blue-green gives an instant, complete switch with an instant switch back. They combine well: canary on the staging slot, then swap.

scenario: The team routes 5% of traffic to a new version for 30 minutes, but nobody checks anything before swapping.
options: A longer canary with no checks
An automated gate comparing the new version's error rate and latency with the old version's, pausing or rolling back if they are worse
Swapping immediately to save time
Asking a tester to click through the site
explanation: The point of a canary is to measure. Comparing SLIs by version in Application Insights, wired into an environment check or protection rule, turns observation into an automatic decision.

scenario: Version 42 renames the CustomerEmail column to Email in the same release. After a problem, the team swaps back to version 41, which fails because the column no longer exists.
options: Never roll back
Expand and contract: add the new column first, have the code write both and read the new one, and remove the old column only in a later release
Rename columns only on weekends
Keep the database in the staging slot
explanation: Code can swap back in seconds, but data cannot. Keeping each schema change compatible with the previous version means a rollback always meets a database it understands. Slots do not include the database.

scenario: After a swap, production traffic starts writing to the test database.
options: The swap happened too quickly
The database connection string was not marked as a slot setting, so it travelled with the code during the swap
The staging slot had too few instances
The canary share was too small
explanation: Settings that belong to an environment - connection strings, endpoints - must be slot settings so they stay with the slot. Unmarked settings move with the swap, taking staging's configuration into production.

scenario: A new recommendations feature is ready in code but the team wants staff to try it for two days, then 10% of shoppers, with a way to turn it off instantly.
stem: What is the most suitable approach?
options: A separate deployment for staff
A dark launch: deploy with the feature behind an App Configuration flag, target staff and then 10%, and use the flag as a kill switch
A long-lived branch merged later
A second production environment
explanation: Flags separate the feature's release from the deployment and allow ring-by-ring exposure and instant disabling. Separate deployments or branches are slower and harder to withdraw.

stem: Why must the API stay compatible with older mobile app versions even when the API can be rolled back instantly?
options: Because mobile apps call a different API
Because installed apps on shoppers' phones cannot be rolled back or forced to update, so the API must keep serving the versions still in use
Because app stores forbid API changes
It does not need to
explanation: Server-side releases can be withdrawn; installed clients cannot. API contracts must stay backward compatible, or be versioned, for as long as older app versions are in use.
